items.summary:
OpenAI filed a lawsuit against Apple in northern California federal court on Friday, accusing the company of stealing its trade secrets and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices. The counterclaims come after Apple sued OpenAI and former employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July for allegedly misappropriating trade secrets to support OpenAI's move into consumer hardware. In its filing, OpenAI said that Apple rehired a former employee who had worked at the company for six months, during which time he gained access to information about a new device as well as OpenAI's roadmap for future products. The company argued that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place.

Apple denied using the rehired employee to access confidential information and rejected claims that it was trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing, calling the counterclaims 'a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit.' The dispute has intensified amid a broader race between the two companies to develop AI products. OpenAI criticized Apple for encouraging employees to do work on personal devices and accounts before preventing orderly separation when they leave, saying that 400 employees have departed Apple for OpenAI so far and that Apple seeks to intimidate others from leaving.
items.title: OpenAI Countersues Apple Over Alleged Trade Secret Theft

items.summary:
Apple plans to open its first company-operated retail store in Hyderabad, named Apple Kukatpally, at Lake Shore-Y Junction Mall on December 10, 2026, at 5 pm. The outlet would become the seventh company-run Apple Store in India and the second in southern India, joining existing stores in Mumbai (two), Delhi-NCR (two), Bengaluru (one), and Pune (one). Hyderabad already hosts Apple's research and development and retail customer care teams, making it another addition to the city's local operations.

The store would feature a pearl-inspired logo reflecting Hyderabad's association with pearls, along with exclusive wallpapers, stickers, and a music playlist celebrating local sounds. It was set to showcase products including the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Duo, as well as MacBooks, Apple Watches, AirPods, and other devices so customers could experience them in person rather than ordering online.

The outlet would also host free 'Today at Apple' sessions covering photography, video creation, and digital drawing, plus provide access to technical experts including Apple's Genius team for product assistance.
items.title: Apple to Open First Hyderabad Store on December 10

items.summary:
Indian textile and apparel exporters are racing to ship goods before new US tariffs take effect, as profit margins have been squeezed by rising raw material prices such as cotton and synthetic yarn. The USTR has proposed a Section 301 tariff ceiling of up to 25% on Indian goods, with a conditional reduced rate of 17% tied to a reciprocal trade agreement that is likely to affect home textiles, furnishings, and apparel exports.

Sanjay Jain, managing director at TT Textile, said shipments for the upcoming spring-summer season are about to begin and exporters plan to rush them into January, though shipping times run two months. Vijay Agarwal, chairman of the Creative Group and former Texprocil chairman, refuted US claims of excess capacity, stating that India's textile sectors have no idle manufacturing capacity because production is geared toward export commitments and a domestic market growing at around 7%. He added that mills and exporters operate with tightly planned schedules, leaving little room to absorb sudden tariff increases or cut prices without harming margins.
items.title: India's textile exporters race the tariff clock

items.summary:
A multi-term DMK MP said that while Congress's support to the delimitation bill is unlikely to automatically lead the party into an alliance with the BJP-led NDA, it does open a path for alignment and offer the national party a fresh opening in Tamil Nadu. The MP noted this development weakens the anti-South charge leveled by DMK, Congress, and others against the BJP.

The delimitation bill makes explicit provision that each state's share of Lok Sabha seats will remain unchanged and freezes the maximum strength of the lower house until 2051, concessions aimed at winning over the DMK. Alongside these measures, BJP has reportedly made subtle moves to dial down its push for other legislative bills drawing sharp opposition from Tamil Nadu, including a slowdown in work by two parliamentary committees overseeing the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill and a Constitution Amendment Bill.

The DMK has long championed state autonomy and decried central government encroachment on its turf, sharply criticizing both bills. The parties share an alliance history: BJP and DMK were allies in the 1999 Lok Sabha elections, with the regional party as part of the Atal Bihari Vajpayee-led government before their split in 2003.

The article suggests that political compulsions may serve as the glue for a potential DMK-BJP alignment, similar to how they worked for Congress and DMK in 2004. With the DMK out of the INDIA bloc and misgivings persisting within sections of its party over joining hands with BJP, which has been a bitter critic of its anti-Hindutva rhetoric, such factors may drive cooperation despite reservations.
items.title: DMK Support to Delimitation Bill Opens Path to BJP Alignment

items.summary:
India is pursuing the first phase of a bilateral trade agreement with the US to protect its export competitiveness amid high American tariffs and to gain an edge over rival South and Southeast Asian manufacturers. The two sides finalised the framework in February 2026 after negotiations launched that same year, but shifting tariff policy has returned them to talks.

The US proposed additional Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies including India (ev2), capping at up to 25 per cent for New Delhi while offering a reduced rate of 17 per cent if the pact is finalised. The USTR's second investigation into structural excess manufacturing capacity cited Indian industrial policies and named sectors such as steel, solar, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and ICT (ev23).

India rejected the allegations, saying it has no structural excess capacity in any sector and that concerns should be handled within trade pact negotiations while remaining committed to early conclusion of the deal. The interim agreement framework would see India cut tariffs on US industrial goods and commit to buying USD 500 billion of US energy products, aircraft parts, precious metals, technology products and coking coal over five years.

Experts caution that even at the proposed rate, India's advantage is narrow: a one per cent edge over Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand under an 18 per cent deal rate (ev23), and only three per cent versus Vietnam and China under a 20 per cent rate. The forced-labour probe covers 60 countries including Pakistan, Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Turkiye, leaving those exporters with relative cost advantages in the US market.

The GTRI think tank urged New Delhi to reject what it calls a one-sided deal while up to 100 per cent Graham tariffs loom. The USTR scheduled public hearings on January 25 and sought written comments by January 5 before any tariffs take effect.
items.title: India-US Trade Pact and Tariffs

items.summary:
Grand Theft Auto 6's developer, Rockstar Games, is confronting a problem as coders and gamers attempt unofficial PC versions of the game using powerful AI tools and leaked files. The move comes even though Rockstar has not yet announced an official PC release; historically it shipped GTA on PC long after its console launch, about 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

The effort is being linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model released in September and agentic tools such as Claude Code. Mark Brown, creator of Game Maker's Toolkit, said cloning takes two forms: replication, which he compared to making a replica painting, and reverse engineering through decompilation or recompilation. Indie developers Sodoj and Marco from Robotonic reported their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appearing on Yandex with the same name and similar mechanics.

Earlier in November, Cyberleek released what they claimed was a near-complete Xbox development build of GTA 6 and later leaked the missing .exe file needed to launch it. Brown said people are now using AI to decompile that build into a PC version, and several groups posted progress on X, with one attempt reportedly running nearly as smoothly as console play on a high-end PC.

Rockstar and its parent Take-Two Interactive have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build or responded to requests for comment. However, Take-Two issued takedown notices against public projects porting the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub, stating there are no remedies available to rectify what it called a clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement.

Legal experts say decompilation sits in a grey area until it reaches the point of infringing copyright or intellectual property. Aaron Treble, a UK IP lawyer for Lewis Silkin, said anyone releasing or selling a clone will almost certainly be infringing on copyright, while Anthropic reportedly told Claude Code to steer away from recreating specific existing games.

Take-Two's chief executive Strauss Zelnick noted that piracy had been less of an issue in video games due to file sizes and complexity. Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said PC versions are often delayed because they must accommodate different hardware configurations rather than a standardized console setup.
items.title: Gamers Use AI and Leaked Files to Clone Grand Theft Auto 6

items.summary:
Canadian Kenneth Law, 61, apologised in court to the families of his victims during a Friday sentencing hearing where prosecutors sought a 25-year prison term. He pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, while admitting he caused dozens of deaths across England and Wales; under a plea deal Canadian authorities withdrew more serious murder charges so that no UK or British death will be prosecuted.

Prosecutors described Law as a predator who exploited vulnerable young people for financial gain. Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty said his victims needed help but found 'Mr Law and his products for death,' adding that he sold to anyone able to pay without considering their circumstances. Defence lawyer Matthew Gourlay countered, arguing each victim's mental illness was its own tragedy and that Law held a misguided belief he was helping them.

Authorities reported the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients met in online suicide forums across 40 countries, roughly a quarter sent to the UK. If Law receives the recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years after credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest; Gourlay has asked for a 12-year term.

Law told the court that words could never replace the families' losses and that he remains remorseful. The hearing followed emotional testimony in September, when grieving family members described the pain Law caused, with those impact statements to be considered at sentencing due later.
items.title: Kenneth Law apologises at sentencing hearing

items.summary:
US President Donald Trump has announced a fresh round of tariffs targeting some of America's largest trading partners, including the European Union, China and Japan. The import taxes are set to affect these countries under new measures.

Hosuk Lee-Makiyama, a Brussels-based trade economist and director of the European Centre for International Political Economy, told Euronews that the tariffs appear designed to revive earlier policy rather than introduce something entirely new. He described the situation as an attempt to bring back previous tariffs under different legislation, stating 'We are not looking at a new shock here.' Lee-Makiyama characterized the measures as a continuation of existing approaches instead of a novel economic disruption.
items.title: Trump Announces New Tariffs on EU, China and Japan

items.summary:
American figure skater Ilia Malinin broke the short program world record at the NHK Trophy on Friday, scoring 114.81 points to surpass Nathan Chen's Olympic mark of 113.97 from the 2022 Beijing Games and his own previous best of 111.29.

Malinin attributed part of his improvement to offseason work on presentation, skating skills, and musical interpretation, and credited the Japanese crowd with helping him deliver a strong performance after expressing surprise at the high score. His program component mark of 46.41 topped the field, addressing an area where he had previously drawn criticism.

He skated to 'Cantata Memoria,' which honors victims of the 1966 Aberfan disaster and those killed in the January 2025 American Airlines Flight 5342 collision near Washington. Shun Sato finished second with 96.78 points, Kevin Aymoz of France third with 94.15, and Russian skaters competing as Individual Neutral Athletes placed eighth and ninth.

The NHK Trophy is the sixth of six Grand Prix qualifying events leading to the Final from Dec. 10 to 13 in Chongqing, China.
items.title: Ilia Malinin Breaks Nathan Chen's Short Program World Record at NHK Trophy

On Saturday, November 28, New Zealand were 330 for eight at lunch on day two of the second Test against India at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. Wicketkeeper Tom Blundell was unbeen on 80 not out and tailender Matt Henry on five not out when play paused.

India took three wickets during that session after New Zealand resumed on 246 for five, having been sent in to bat following the toss loss. Fast bowler Anshul Kamboj struck first by catching Glenn Phillips behind for 36, and Akash Deep claimed his third wicket of the innings with a caught-and-bowled dismissal of Nathan Smith for 26 before removing Kyle Jamieson for 19, Yashasvi Jaiswal taking a diving catch at deep midwicket. Kamboj was denied a fifth wicket just before lunch when Devdutt Padikkal spilled the catch in the gully after it pinged off Henry's glove.

With the first Test in Wellington drawn, Christchurch carries significant implications for both teams' World Test Championship final hopes: India must win to keep their chances alive, while New Zealand cannot afford a loss as they seek to stay close to leading South Africa and Australia.
items.title: New Zealand reach 330/8 at lunch in second test against India

items.summary:
Jamaica qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil with a 3-0 win over Costa Rica in the CONCACAF W Championship quarter-finals on Friday, November 27. The match took place at Mansfield, Texas, where Jamaica controlled play from the start and booked their third consecutive appearance at the tournament.

Jody Brown opened the scoring in the 16th minute with a close-range finish after a pass from Kalyssa Van Zanten. Van Zanten then finished off a well-worked team move in the 59th minute, assisted by captain Khadija Shaw on her 50th international appearance. Shaw completed the victory six minutes later with a free kick that took a deflection off the Costa Rica wall.

Jamaica previously qualified for the tournaments in 2019 and 2023, reaching the round of 16 in 2023 as their best performance. The four quarter-final winners qualify directly for the tournament, while the losers will play on Wednesday for a chance to advance to the intercontinental playoffs.

In Tuesday's semi-finals, Jamaica will face the winner of Friday's other quarter-final between defending champions United States and El Salvador. Canada are set to face Panama and Mexico meet Haiti in Saturday's remaining quarter-finals.
items.title: Jamaica Rout Costa Rica to Secure Women's World Cup Berth

This week's Finshots wrapup examines several Indian economic topics, including why the convenience store chain 7-Eleven failed in India despite partnering first with Future Group and later Reliance. The piece also addresses why Indian Railways is abandoning its Tatkal booking quota even as it launched Vande Bharat Sleeper trains without a Tatkal option, noting that passenger services posted an operating loss of ₹63,721 crore in FY25.

The wrapup questions whether India still needs broad free foodgrain distribution given rapid poverty reduction, while explaining reasons the government is hesitant to shrink the scheme despite concerns about beneficiaries who may not need assistance. It also reports that Bangladesh and Nepal requested three more years as least developed countries after being due for graduation this week, citing trade benefits and international support.

Finally, the piece highlights SpiceJet's steep decline in an industry expected to expand sharply, with domestic market share falling from about 21% in July 2014 to just 0.6% by September 2026 against a government projection of passenger traffic growing sixfold to around 1.1 billion by 2040.

The wrapup also announces the top scorers of Finshots' weekly quiz, with nine participants tied for merch eligibility and a tie-breaker question sent to the 'Bulls', while this week's quiz remains open until noon on Friday, December 4, 2026.
items.title: Finshots Weekly Wrapup Covers SpiceJet's Decline and Other Economic Topics

According to Adobe Analytics, US shoppers are projected to spend more than $13 billion online on Black Friday as bargain-hunting consumers look past inflation and high gas prices. Spending reached $9.7 billion through 6:30 p.m. ET, up 12.8 per cent from the prior year, with a final total expected between $13 billion and $13.4 billion.

Adobe expects spending to stay strong over the weekend, forecasting Saturday at $6.1 billion (up 6 per cent) and Sunday at $6.4 billion (up 7.5 per cent). Cyber Monday is projected as the season's largest online shopping day with $15.1 billion in spending, up 6.2 per cent year over year, while the five-day stretch from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday should rise 7.4 per cent to $47.5 billion.

Separate Salesforce data showed Black Friday US online sales generated $5.9 billion and $30.7 billion globally in the first half of the day, keeping it on track for projected spending of $18.7 billion in the US (a 4 per cent year-over-year increase) and a rise to $83 billion worldwide (up 5.2 per cent). Adobe had forecast earlier that Black Friday online sales would grow 9.2 per cent to $12.9 billion, and it now expects overall US holiday online spending this year to expand at a similar pace to last year's.
items.title: Adobe Forecasts Record Black Friday Online Sales Above $13 Billion

According to Goodreturns data, petrol and diesel prices remained largely stable across major Indian cities on November 28, with Gurgaon and Noida recording reductions in both fuels while Thiruvananthapuram saw a marginal increase in diesel. In Gurgaon, petrol fell by ₹0.20 per litre to ₹102.77 and diesel dropped by ₹0.20 to ₹95.44; in Noida, petrol declined by ₹0.16 to ₹101.96 while diesel fell by ₹0.12 to ₹95.44.

Diesel prices in Thiruvananthapuram rose marginally by ₹0.01 to ₹104.41 per litre, Goodreturns reported. Separately, Bloomberg noted that Brent crude oil fell around 1% on Friday to settle near $95 a barrel while still recording a weekly gain amid Middle East attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers as the Iran conflict entered its tenth month.

The International Energy Agency expects the global oil market to move into surplus this quarter despite persistent geopolitical tensions. Dennis Kissler, senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc., told Bloomberg that traders remain focused on Strait of Hormuz attacks keeping a bid under prices while volumes indicate an oversupplied market. Traders are also watching an upcoming OPEC meeting where members remain divided over sustainable production levels.

Bloomberg reported that diesel futures in Europe and US retail fuel prices have declined from earlier peaks, offering some relief to oil-product markets. Rising international energy prices are increasing India's import bill given the country's dependence on imported crude oil and natural gas. Tarun Kapoor, adviser in the Prime Minister's Office speaking at the 16th Energy Security Conference organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), said high crude and gas prices have added an estimated ₹6-7 lakh crore annually to India's financial burden.

Kapoor called for a structural shift towards electric vehicles in freight and passenger transportation to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, warning that heavy reliance on energy imports leaves the economy vulnerable to international price shocks. He noted India imported 122.7 million tonnes of crude oil during the first half of the 2026-27 financial year, marginally higher than the 121.8 MT imported in the corresponding period a year earlier.
items.title: Petrol and Diesel Prices Stable Across Indian Cities on November 28

The author released version 0.4a0 of the datasette-charts plugin on 27th November 2026, which addresses friction points in building additional chart types through a dedicated plugin hook that lets other plugins define new charts. To test this hook, Claude Opus 5.5 built an experimental plugin that surfaced several design problems; this release resolves those issues with the goal of making it considerably more ergonomic to create further chart plugins.

The author also added a website for the plugin at charts.datasette.io. The site includes a tutorial aimed at plugin authors and a gallery displaying all core charts and annotations, each linking to an interactive demo on Datasette Lite.
items.title: Datasette Releases datasette-charts Plugin Version 0.4a0

The National Energy Regulator of South Africa (NERSA) issued a guidance notice on November 26, 2026, outlining requirements and submission deadlines for licensed municipal and private electricity distributors preparing cost of supply studies and tariff applications for the 2027/28 financial year. The notice aims to support regulatory compliance and improve the quality of tariff submissions.

Distributors must submit their cost of supply studies for preliminary verification by February 1, 2027, with complete tariff applications reaching NERSA by March 20, 2027, in accordance with an operative court order. The regulator is scheduled to issue its decisions by May 5, 2027.

NERSA clarified that distributors must prepare their cost of supply studies using the Rate of Return Methodology applicable to the 2027/28 financial year and comply with the amended Electricity Regulation Act, 2006, relevant provisions of the existing Cost of Supply Framework and Pricing Methodology, prescribed distribution forms known as D-forms, and ring-fenced electricity financial records. The regulator encouraged distributors to provide comprehensive supporting information demonstrating the relationship between underlying data, revenue requirements, and proposed tariffs.

Key required information includes audited financial statements, depreciated regulatory asset base figures, explanations of prudent operating costs, revenue recovery mechanisms, cost allocation approaches, cross-subsidy arrangements, energy losses, and service efficiency. Applications will be evaluated against applicable legislation, pricing policies, licence conditions, approved methodologies, and relevant court orders.

NERSA highlighted the importance of public participation under the National Energy Regulator Act and the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act, encouraging distributors to prepare public versions of their cost of supply studies and tariff applications with sufficient supporting information to enable meaningful stakeholder participation in the regulatory process.
items.title: NERSA Sets February and March 2027 Deadlines for South Africa's 2027/28 Electricity Tariff Applications

The US government announced that internet bandwidth provider RETN is being barred from US networks, according to a notice posted to the Federal Register on Friday. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security stated in the notice that RETN poses 'undue and unacceptable risks' as identified in a 2019 executive order concerning hostile foreign IT firms.

The notice requires RETN and its successors to decommission and remove all equipment it has provided or installed, either directly or through third parties, from any US network, and to terminate services provided to US persons. These actions are set to take effect on January 1, 2027.

RETN describes itself as a 'Eurasian Network' with cables connecting Europe and Asia via Russia, while a 2013 press release characterized the company as 'a leading Russian wholesale telecom and backbone provider.' Reuters was unable to reach RETN for comment at the time of reporting.
items.title: US Bars Bandwidth Provider RETN from American Networks

IONNA is running a holiday promotion on its fast-charging network, offering charging at half price until the end of Sunday, November 29. The sale rate comes to $0.20 per kWh plus tax, down from IONNA's regular capped network-wide rate of $0.39 per kWh, which requires no paid membership.

The discount applies across its entire fast-charging network for any compatible EV. As an example, adding 50 kWh ordinarily costs up to $19.50 before tax at an IONNA charger, but during the sale it will cost $10, a savings of $9.50.

Automakers that founded IONNA have added their own discounts on top of this weekend deal; drivers of those vehicles can stack them by starting their session through their automaker's app or Plug & Charge. IONNA's Rechargeries provide both NACS and CCS connectors with speeds up to 400 kW, and its locator shows locations, live availability, connector types, amenities, and which makes and models qualify for the extra Plug & Charge discounts.

The piece also includes an unrelated EnergySage advertisement promoting solar installation services.

ZDNET reports a Black Friday deal on the wireless PlayStation DualSense controller at Amazon that knocks $21 off, bringing the price to $54. The source states this represents a 28% discount and matches the all-time low for the basic white variant, with other colors also available while retailers like Best Buy and Target offer discounts as well.

The item is described as the standard controller that ships with the PlayStation 5 and supports wireless connectivity with the PS5, Mac, and PC. It features haptics, adaptive triggers, an accelerometer, gyroscope, built-in microphone, a 3.5mm jack for headsets, USB-C charging, and battery life of around six to ten hours.

ZDNET assigns this deal a rating of 3 out of 5 on its system, noting that the PS5 controllers do not go on sale very often and that Amazon's Black Friday sale ends Nov. 30 without a set expiration for this offer. The outlet frames itself as committed to sourcing and updating deals through expert monitoring.

ZDNET also explains how it rates deals, stating in 2025 it developed a measurable system combining a percentage-off classification with a sliding scale based on factors such as frequency, brand, product recognition, and team expertise. It claims 33 years of experience, 30 hands-on product reviewers, and 10,000 square feet of lab space to back its recommendations.

New research published in Science Advances estimates that sinking land and rising seas could expose more than seven million people living in Africa's coastal megacities to flooding by mid-century. The analysis combines satellite data with sea level rise projections to assess flood risk across 20 of the continent's most populous coastal cities (ev1).

Under a moderate warming scenario, an extreme short-term sea level event could expose about a million buildings and $180bn in assets to flooding (ev2). In Lagos, Nigeria, and Alexandria, Egypt alone, five million people and $150bn in assets could be exposed by mid-century (ev3).

The researchers combined more than 4,000 satellite images of Africa's coastline to measure how quickly different regions are rising or sinking (ev4). They identified Lagos and Alexandria as subsidence hotspots, finding the two cities sink at rates of 5.2mm and 6.3mm per year respectively (ev5, ev6), comparable to south-east Asian megacities such as Jakarta, Manila and Ho Chi Minh City.

The authors combined these estimates with sea level rise projections from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change's sixth assessment report under three emissions scenarios, using 2020 population data, building footprints and GDP per capita to estimate exposure over the 21st century (dt7). They held city populations constant at 2020 levels so they could isolate the effects of sea level rise and vertical land movement on flood risk.

While Lagos and Alexandria are most vulnerable, Djibouti City in Djibouti, Mogadishu in Somalia and Tripoli in Libya would face minimal economic exposure due to their smaller populations and infrastructure bases. Subsidence in African coastal cities has not been consistently monitored before this study, largely because of a lack of local data.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho, a PhD student at Virginia Tech, told Carbon Brief that the analysis keeps population and city data constant so it can isolate sea level rise effects; if people move away from threatened areas over coming decades estimates could be too high, but continued urban growth could make them too low. He also noted the flood model assumes no coastal defenses, making it a worst-case physical picture.

Africa is the world's fastest-urbanising region, with cities growing at an average rate of 3.5% every year (ev9). By 2050, Africa's urban population is expected to double from 7m to 1.4bn (dt10, ev11, ev12). The authors say their satellite method could be used in other data-scarce coastal regions across the global south.
items.title: Sinking African Megacities Could Expose Seven Million People to Flooding by 2050

On Friday, the opposition faced a possible passage of the delimitation bill after both DMK and NCP (SP), parties that had been critical to its defeat in April, signalled willingness to back the legislation. Congress responded by alleging that BJP sought to 'change the Constitution' through delimitation following what it called an unsuccessful election outcome, claiming the redrawing of Lok Sabha seats would be handled by a compromised Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who had allegedly been exposed for manipulating electoral rolls. AICC general secretary KC Venugopal vowed to expose BJP and stated that Modi and Shah intended 'to set a big trap against the people of India,' describing it as the design behind the episode.

Despite these accusations, opposition mood was despondent as confidence in unity among anti-bill ranks dissipated following statements from M K Stalin and NCP (SP) leaders. Regret emerged over Congress's decision to abruptly drop its ally DMK in favour of TVK when forming a government in Tamil Nadu, angering the Dravidian party into drifting toward BJP while Congress leaders attacked DMK on Friday amid queries about whether TN Congress members regretted leaving the alliance.

Ahead of Parliament's special sitting, BJD said party president Naveen Patnaik would take the final call on both delimitation and women's reservation bills. Manas Mangaraj stated that decisions would be guided by Odisha's interests once details were clear, though he did not confirm a decision had been made.
items.title: Opposition Despondent as DMK and NCP Signal Support for Delimitation Bill

The Commerce Department's Census Bureau reported on Friday that the US goods trade deficit widened by 10.7%, or $14.4 billion, to $149.5 billion in October. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast a smaller shortfall of about $133 billion for the month.

Goods imports rose sharply by $21.1 billion to $365.3 billion while exports increased more modestly by $6.7 billion to $215.8 billion, leaving the deficit substantially larger than expected. Separately reported on Wednesday, trade reduced third-quarter GDP growth by 3.21 percentage points, but that drag was offset by strong consumer spending and business investment in equipment, much of it AI-related.

The economy expanded at a 4.3% annualized rate last quarter after growing at 2.2% during the April-June period. Trade has not contributed to GDP growth for four straight quarters as domestic demand remains robust.
items.title: US Goods Trade Deficit Widened Sharply in October

A live blog covering Victorian's election day reported the Coalition seeking to topple Labor, with leaders casting votes amid a wave of disaffection toward the incumbent government. Greens leader Ellen Sandell told ABC's Weekend Breakfast that voters are dismayed by how Labor has moved away from its traditional values and followed the Liberals down what she called a rightwing path, prompting people to vote for a progressive voice.

Premier Ben Carroll voted at St Christophers primary school in Airport West while Liberal leader Jess Wilson cast her ballot at Our Lady of Good Counsel in Deepdene. Wilson described herself as confident of statewide victory and said it was not about becoming the first elected female premier or youngest Victorian leader, whereas Carroll credited voters for feeling they had been sold down the river by a radical privatization agenda around kinder, renewables and water.

Polls suggested the Coalition would comfortably win majority government after Labor's 12 years in power. A YouGov poll of more than 4300 voters commissioned by the Herald Sun and News24 put the Coalition at 57.5% to Labor's 42.5%, up from a 55-45 lead in October, while Newspoll reported by The Australian had the Coalition extending to a 15-point two-party preferred lead.

The same YouGov analysis projected One Nation gaining 12 seats and the Greens adding five MPs to their three-member pack, with the Greens expected to take between 13% and 17% of primary votes in what would be their most successful campaign on record. Sandell had received the second-highest approval rating among undecided voters during the four-way leaders debate on 17 November.

More than 2.2 million people had already voted as of Friday, meaning nearly half of eligible voters had cast ballots despite rain and flood warnings across parts of Victoria.
items.title: Victorian Coalition Poised for Majority as Greens Surge

The program 'Tech Now' presents an episode list titled 'Space Travel: Mission Autonomous,' featuring a series of short segments exploring technology across diverse fields. Each listed item is described as approximately 24 to 25 minutes long.

Among the episodes are Alasdair Keane's report from Naples on how tech transforms America's Cup sailing, Yasmin Morgan-Griffiths following an AI early warning team for landslides, and Shiona McCallum visiting Cairngorms National Park to monitor wildfire damage. Other segments include a Pokémon World Championships visit in San Francisco, counterfeit-product detection technology explored by Ammie Sekhon, NASA eclipse research in Iceland tracked by Adrienne Murray, and trials of an assisted birth innovation met with mums and hospital staff.

Additional episodes cover gaming and events such as Gamescom highlights from Laura Cress, the Esports World Cup in Paris, WWE's behind-the-scenes technology examined by Ammie Sekhon, a visit to Microsoft's Quantum Lab in Denmark for supercomputer research, warship preservation work in Sweden, Fifa's new tech at its Zurich headquarters, prosthetics trials discussed with a medical expert, 3D imaging supporting heart surgery explored by Adrienne Murray, underwater endurance trials led by Andrew Rogers, and AI applied to an art history mystery found by Harriet Bradshaw. items.summary:
Vithabai Narayangaonkar was one of Maharashtra's most celebrated performers in Tamasha, the state's traditional travelling folk theatre. Born during a performance in 1935 and joining her father's troupe as a teenager, she became its star after taking over following his death.

Her fame extended beyond Maharashtra; three months after giving birth she performed for soldiers at India's frontier with China in 1962. She refused film offers from filmmakers including Raj Kapoor because the troupe supported around 50 families and would benefit only her personally, according to her daughter Mangala Bansode.

Fans demonstrated their devotion during a Diwali performance in Mumbai in 1971 when spectators insisted on buying tickets as gifts even though rain cancelled the show. Her fortunes declined later; her husband Maruti Sawant mismanaged finances and took loans in her name, leaving her heavily indebted by 1982.

She disbanded her troupe in 1990 but received the Sangeet Natak Akademi Award that same year and campaigned for pensions. Her financial struggles continued until she died in January 2002; her family could pay only 4,000 of the 5,900 rupees owed to the Pune hospital where she was treated.

Her life has inspired a Bollywood musical called Eetha starring Shraddha Kapoor. Director Laxman Utekar said it is not a biopic but renamed her Vithabai Bhau Gavkar rather than using Mang Narayangaonkar, drawing criticism from writer Pradnya Daya Pawar who argued the change erased references to caste and struggle.

Bansode defended the film regardless of the name. She recalled watching her mother perform while wearing musical anklets weighing 4kg each. Maharashtra has since instituted a lifetime achievement award in Vithabai's name.
items.title: The Indian 'Tamasha queen' whose fans paid for a show that never happened

Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said on Friday that the trade deal between India and the US is close to culmination, describing it as a breakthrough in talks between the two countries. He noted that the process and pathway which had previously held back finalising the deal was now taking shape, with the agreement set to be signed once the US tariff framework is in place.

Goyal said he hoped India would gain a comparative advantage over competitor nations such as Bangladesh, Vietnam, Pakistan, Indonesia, Thailand, and China by securing lower US import tariffs and better market access. His comments followed the latest US Trade Representative's report proposing 25 per cent tariffs on imports from India, with a provision to cap them at 17 per cent if the two countries agree to a bilateral trade deal.

Trade experts expressed hope that the USTR Section 301 report may spur intensive negotiations on the agreement in the coming weeks. Goyal also said he expected the forthcoming EU free trade agreement to be signed later this year and come into effect by March or April next year, while noting India's goods and services exports are on track to achieve a $1 trillion target for the current fiscal.

He added that India is finalising free trade agreements and reforming the GST system to make it simpler, arguing that given the size of the Indian economy, fluctuations in oil prices would not determine its future over the next 20 to 30 years. He also said interest rates remain moderate and suggested more people are waiting for an increase than a reduction ahead of the RBI monetary policy meeting scheduled about a week later.
items.title: India-US Trade Deal Close To Culmination, Piyush Goyal Says

Shoaib Daniyal's India Fix newsletter argues that replacing English place names with their Bengali equivalents is a hollow exercise in decolonisation that undermines national unity. The author traces this debate to the Constituent Assembly, where members clashed over Hindi replacing English as the official language; after accepting both languages with a 15-year sunset period for English, nothing changed once the period ended because Tamil protests kept it in place, and Daniyal cites Pakistan's 1971 split partly over Urdu status as evidence that retaining English was one of India's wisest decisions. He contends that Hindi chauvinists wrongly frame English purely as a colonial import when Indian leaders recognised it had become a local language essential for unity across the country's linguistic diversity.

Daniyal criticises politicians' trend of discarding British-era names, listing Bombay, Madras, Bangalore, Calcutta, Orissa and West Bengal, noting that 'Poschim Bongo,' the Bengali name he says has been used since 1947 when the state was created after the second partition of Bengal, is more than seven decades old. He dismisses this renaming as an easy distraction for politicians seeking to shore up nativist pride while diverting attention from negative news cycles and substantive issues like law and order or mass exclusion of citizens from voter rolls in West Bengal under its new government.

The author frames English as a necessary lingua franca, comparing it to Persian and Sanskrit before it, that enables Indians to communicate across the country's diverse tongues and conducts much of India's intellectual life. He notes this status is unique because most other countries let mass vernaculars occupy all spaces from popular to intellectual domains, whereas India has not achieved this, causing problems such as an inability to deliver quality education in local languages despite experts agreeing children should be taught in their mother tongue.

Daniyal argues that if India truly wanted to move away from English rather than through meaningless name changes, primary school education would create the most impact because Indian children learn very little and high-quality instruction in their mother tongue could help. He points to China's mass network of non-English-medium primary schools as an example he says now leads in cutting-edge technology like artificial intelligence.

Finally, Daniyal contends that India's failures combined with English's allure have pushed parents toward low-quality private schooling bearing a fake 'English-medium' stamp, since classes are not actually conducted in English except at elite institutions yet students still read English textbooks and write exams in English. He highlights additional hollow anti-English posturing through road safety signs, flight safety information rarely available in Bengali for flights to Bengal, and medical labels that almost never include Bengali, calling these serious safety lapses given only a small minority know English.

The author concludes by asserting it is easier for West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari to force non-Bengalis to pronounce 'poshe-chim bawn-go' than to do real work helping the Bengali language and its speakers.}
items.title: Opinion: Renaming Places After the British Undermines Indian Unity

NT Police are investigating the death of a 47-year-old man following an alleged altercation at a property near Pine Creek, about three hours' drive south-east of Darwin. According to police, the man was struck in the head during an incident involving another man yesterday afternoon and taken by family members to Pine Creek Clinic.

At around 5pm clinic staff reported the alleged assault to police, after which the injured man became unresponsive and CPR was commenced. He was declared dead at about 6pm last night. A police spokesperson said investigators were examining whether the incident was domestic violence related and had established a crime scene at the clinic while working to locate the alleged offender.

Police stated that investigations remain ongoing and urged anyone with information about the alleged assault to come forward, providing a contact number of 131444.

The National Biosecurity Committee decided on Friday against listing buffel grass as a weed of national significance, citing divergent stakeholder views and actions already taken in some jurisdictions that prevented reaching national consensus. The fast-spreading, fire-fuelling species was first introduced by Afghan cameleers and intentionally spread from the 1960s to control soil erosion and feed cattle before becoming present across Australia; it is drought-resistant and was declared a weed in the Northern Territory in 2024.

The decision has drawn mixed reactions. Romy Carey, chief executive of the Northern Territory Cattlemen's Association, called it welcome news for pastoralists who rely on buffel as pasture, while acknowledging its environmental risks and supporting targeted control where needed. Environmental groups and Indigenous land managers criticized the outcome as short-sighted; Taigen Ryan of the Invasive Species Council said the decision exposed a failure in Australia's biosecurity system that let vested interests outweigh the environment, though she noted listing would not have removed pastoralists' use of the grass.

Ryan called for a federal inquiry into the inadequate national response to buffel and its threats to ecosystems, culturally significant sites, health, and infrastructure. Her call was echoed by the Arid Land Environment Centre and the Central Land Council; CLC Indigenous land manager Garth Forrester said without coordinated management resources meant for caring for people would instead be spent on weed control, noting that buffel ticks all boxes for listing as a threat to culture, health, and infrastructure. The Invasive Species Council is also seeking a broader national inquiry into the grass's impacts across these areas.
items.title: Buffel Grass Not Named Weed of National Significance

items.summary:
As Spain's Popular Party (PP) closes its election campaign, leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo publicly appeals to left-wing voters for their support even though the party expects to govern with far-right Vox. At a closing rally in Seville backed by Andalusian President Juan Manuel Moreno, Feijóo addressed roughly 9,000 supporters and asked them directly not to abandon him over corruption concerns.

The PP's strategy contains an acknowledged paradox: it courts the left while privately assuming its majority depends on Vox. Party officials explained that the goal is simply 'not to leave the center to the PSOE' rather than competing with a party they expect to govern alongside anyway. Moreno framed the appeal as about Spain and national dignity, urging voters who lent their support in May 2022 to do so again.

According to PP tracking polls, the party expects between 130 and 135 seats, down from its 2023 result of 137. Vox is projected at around 55 seats compared with its current 32. The combined right-wing total would exceed an absolute majority while the PSOE trails well behind.

Feijóo's appeal follows a campaign split between strong debate performances and recent controversies, including his use of 'calladita' toward Ada Colau during Thursday's four-way debate. Despite these setbacks, PP leaders maintain high expectations that their combined seats will secure government.
items.title: Feijóo Courts Left Voters While Counting on Right-Wing Majority

items.summary:
Pedro Sánchez ended his sixth PSOE campaign with the largest rally of his career, drawing more than 13,000 people into Madrid's Caja Mágica beyond capacity. He framed the election as a fight over rights and jobs rather than a personal referendum against him, contrasting a welfare-state government with one he called 'the government of scissors and chainsaws.' The event took place at the venue rechristened the Caja Roja (Red Box), where speakers included Ángela Raya, who spoke after her grandfather's remains were recovered in 2025 following an 89-year search. Sánchez said sources at La Moncloa aim for around 35% of the vote to win roughly 140 seats and reach the 176 needed with partners for an absolute majority, even though most polls place them outside government.

The rally emphasized social messages rather than corruption scandals or campaign failures. Sánchez seized on Feijóo's remark telling Ada Colau 'keep quiet,' arguing that women voters would respond by voting loudly in a Spain of 2026. He invoked figures like Nevenka Fernández, who reported harassment in 2001 and led to an equality law six years later, and Ana Orantes, whose murder followed her denouncing gender violence before the comprehensive law against it passed. Sánchez demanded 75% turnout to stop what he called the regression represented by Feijóo and Abascal, championed same-sex marriage and right-to-die laws that Vox ignores while Feijóo intends to repeal euthanasia legislation, and even claimed victory by demanding the PP accept whatever result emerges on November 29.
items.title: Sánchez Closes Sixth Campaign With Record Rally and Claims Victory

The Supreme Court directed that the ceremonial Karthigai Deepam be lit atop the Deepathoon stone pillar on Thiruparankundram Hill in Madurai, Tamil Nadu. Morning visuals captured from the Subramaniya Swami Temple followed this fresh order issued by the court.

This directive came after non-compliance with an earlier November 20 Supreme Court order that had permitted a one-time lighting of the lamp on Thiruparankundram Hill. The ceremonial lamp remained unlit on November 24 despite those prior directions, prompting the new ruling.
items.title: Supreme Court Orders Deepathoon Lamp Lighting at Thiruparankundram

Andhra Pradesh chief minister N Chandrababu Naidu urged the Opposition to support the Centre's proposed delimitation legislation, warning parties against being on the wrong side of history by blocking women's reservation. At a New Delhi press conference he defended the proposal to increase Lok Sabha seats by 50% across all states as a win-win that would protect southern states' representation while enabling a 33% reservation for women in both houses.

Kumaraswamy, echoing Naidu, said every southern state including Karnataka and Kerala would see its constituencies rise by the same proportion once implemented. He accused Congress of creating confusion over delimitation and taking no clear position on women's reservation, warning voters would not forgive parties that oppose the bills while expressing confidence they could pass by voice vote.

Naidu argued linking seat expansion with women's quota prevents men's existing representation from shrinking if seats stayed at 543. He cited calculations showing the population per parliamentarian falling from around 2.7-2.8 million to about 1.8 million after the expansion, and appealed directly to women to pressure parties for their rights.

The Union Cabinet cleared the revised constitutional amendment proposal ahead of a special Parliament sitting beginning November 30.
items.title: Naidu and Kumaraswamy Back 50% Lok Sabha Expansion

The Union government plans for a Supreme Court judge, whether sitting or retired and appointed by the Central Government, to serve as Chairperson of the proposed Delimitation Commission. According to the Delimitation Bill 2026 that is set to be introduced in an upcoming special session of Parliament, the commission will comprise three primary members: this chairperson; the Chief Election Commissioner (or a nominated Election Commissioner); and the State Election Commissioner of the relevant state.

The bill states that the Commission would be formed soon after Parliament passes it. The Delimitation Bill references Article 243K for appointing the State Election Commissioner, with Governor-nominated persons acting in this role for Meghalaya and Nagaland. A senior government official said special provisions apply to Jammu and Kashmir as a Union Territory, that the commission would be constituted immediately after bill passage, and that reservation would be implemented for the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.

The same official noted that states will clear the constitutional amendment bill simultaneously, with about half of them ratifying it since ratification is treated as convention rather than a requirement. The government intends to decide through notification how long the Commission may function, and an extension could be granted if requested by the commission or deemed necessary.
items.title: Supreme Court Judge to Head Delimitation Commission Panel

The Centre has proposed a bill to implement one-third reservation for women, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, by raising the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 members. The Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026 is slated for introduction in the Lok Sabha on Monday, with up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories.

The proposal calls for a 50 per cent increase in seats across both houses of Parliament and state Legislative Assemblies, over and above existing numbers. State Assembly size would rise from 500 to 650, with revised seat allocations and constituency boundaries remaining fixed until the year 2051.

The Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons states that the quota would run for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment, with Parliament empowered to extend it by law. The new measure would trigger the quota after the first delimitation under the proposed amendment, using the latest published census figures available at its commencement to redraw constituency boundaries.

WWE announced on Saturday that wrestler Jermaine Haley, known by his ring name Bronson Reed, died at age 38 due to medical complications. The company posted a statement expressing grief and paying tribute to the Australian performer as 'a larger-than-life figure in WWE' while emphasizing he was also 'a phenomenal person, a devoted family man,' extending condolences to his entire family including pregnant wife Paige, their daughter, friends, co-workers, and fans.

Reed's final appearance occurred at Crown Jewel in Saudi Arabia during the World Tag Team Championship match between Bron Breakker and Austin Theory versus Penta and Je'Von Evans. He attempted to assist Breakker and Theory before Oba Femi intervened, sending Reed crashing through a table; this spot reportedly left him with serious injuries including broken ribs and a lacerated kidney.

Reed remained in Saudi Arabia for medical treatment before returning to the United States, and WWE had earlier acknowledged that he was hospitalized following the Crown Jewel incident. The company has not disclosed whether his reported injuries were connected to the medical complications that led to his death.
items.title: WWE Announces Death of Star Bronson Reed at 38

Voters across 22 cities and counties went to the polls on Saturday, with polling stations open from 8 am until a scheduled closing at 4 pm local time. The elections elected mayors, county chiefs, council members, and other local representatives whose four-year terms will begin after results are tallied later in the day.

Analysts say the contest could signal party support ahead of Taiwan's 2028 presidential election while China monitors the outcome. Campaigning focused largely on local issues such as transport and the environment, though tensions with Beijing remained a backdrop; President Lai Ching-te campaigned for Democratic Progressive Party candidates at a rally in Taoyuan City.

The main race pits the ruling DPP against the opposition Kuomintang, which won 14 cities and counties while the DPP secured five in the 2022 vote. Taipei's mayoral contest drew particular attention as incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an faces DPP candidate Puma Shen, whom China has denounced and says is wanted for separatism; Shen told Reuters that Chinese police had never contacted him.

The security backdrop intensified after Taiwan's Defence Ministry reported detecting 30 Chinese military aircraft around the island on Friday, with 26 crossing the strait's median line during a joint combat readiness patrol involving warships. The government warned voters to stay alert to social media claims it described as continuing Chinese disinformation efforts.
items.title: Taiwan Votes in High-Stakes Local Elections as China Watches Closely

The Supreme Court's November 20 order permitted the Karthigai lamp at the Deepathoon on Thirupparankundram hill to be lit on November 24 as a one-time measure, and paragraph 16 of that order bars every party from relying on the permission or ceremony as evidence of custom, usage, or possession. The bench added that no later year may invoke the arrangement for a similar request, though the bar runs only until adjudication of pending appeals listed for January 2027.

The article tests whether such clauses hold by surveying earlier arrangements at contested shrines. At Ayodhya, an interim injunction granted on January 16, 1950 governed the site until a Supreme Court decision in M Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das (2019), nearly seven decades later. At Gyanvapi mosque in Varanasi, permission for puja in a cellar permitted on January 31, 2024 continues because the case remains pending after the court declined to stay it on April 1, 2024.

At Aland dargah in Karnataka's Kalaburagi district, February 2025 permission for 15 people to perform Mahashivratri puja against a request for 500 became an annual application after petitioners kept returning; the Supreme Court declined under Article 32 and left it with the High Court. At Shringar Gauri shrine on Gyanvapi's outer wall, once-a-year worship permitted by administration supported five women's August 2021 suit for daily worship that led to a 2022 survey of the premises.

At Bhojshala-Kamal Maula Mosque complex in Dhar, an ASI order dated April 7, 2003 allowed Hindu worship on Tuesdays and namaz on Fridays until the Madhya Pradesh High Court declared the complex a temple on May 15, 2026; the Supreme Court declined to stay that ruling and directed open space for Friday prayers. At Thirupparankundram itself, an arrangement lit at the traditional mandapam held since November 1996 did not prevent the High Court in 2025 from directing the lamp to the Deepathoon.

The Supreme Court has also declined first-time observances on festival eve, ordering status quo at Idgah Maidan in Bengaluru's Chamarajpet on August 30, 2022. The article notes these cases differ: there state permission and disputed title stood behind the interim order, whereas two High Court rulings favored devotees before the January 6, 2026 bench direction.

The record shows no instance of a court treating its own interim permission as proof of custom; instead arrangements tend to last as long as litigation, single-occasion permissions invite fresh applications, and limited concessions can underpin wider claims. Tamil Nadu's November 21 review petition argued clarifications cannot undo the factual consequence of the ceremony performed under court authority.

The promise in paragraph 16 will be kept or broken by the calendar: a final judgment before the next Karthigai would leave November 24, 2026 as the sole occasion described, whereas appeals still pending in November 2027 would face the same request on the same reasoning.
items.title: Deepathoon row: Why interim orders at disputed shrines seldom stay interim

items.summary:
Russia is seeking a prisoner swap involving Letícia 'Lelê' Villar, a Brazilian beach soccer player jailed since July 2025 for bringing hashish into the country, in exchange for Sergey Cherkasov, an alleged Russian spy serving a five-year sentence in Brazil. According to an official who asked not to be identified because of private matters, the swap would free Villar and release Cherkasov from his term.

Cherkasov was arrested in Brazil in 2022 after Dutch authorities denied him entry while he sought an internship at the International Criminal Court using a false Brazilian identity. In 2023, the US charged him with acting as an agent of a Russian intelligence service and requested his extradition; Villar had used the alias Victor Muller Ferreira when pursuing graduate studies at Johns Hopkins University before moving to Brazil on her passport. Brazilian police found no evidence that Cherkasov spied on the government, companies or institutions.

Brazil rejected a US request to extradite Cherkasov after its Supreme Court approved his eventual transfer to Russia pending completion of proceedings in Brazil, and separately ordered him expelled once he finishes serving his sentence or is released by the judiciary. Villar has appealed directly to President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva for help securing her release, writing this month that she feels suffering from being detained; Brazil's foreign affairs ministry said it was following the situation and providing consular assistance while its Justice Ministry declined to comment on ongoing cases.

Villar is not the first prominent athlete whose Russian detention has become entangled in a prisoner exchange: American basketball star Brittney Griner was released in a one-for-one swap in 2022 for Russian arms dealer Viktor Bout after being sentenced to nine years over cannabis oil found in her luggage. Lula's pragmatic relationship with Putin, including more than an hour of phone conversation between the two leaders in August, may give Brazil room to navigate the dispute.
items.title: Brazilian Beach Soccer Star Drawn Into Russia-US Spy Dispute

A group of international scholars traveled across several innovation hubs in Beijing to observe firsthand how the country is pursuing modernization, according to a piece that frames their visit as an effort to understand what other nations can learn from one another while developing distinct approaches. The researchers toured three specific sites: the Zhongguancun National Innovation Demonstration Zone Exhibition Center, the Digital and Intelligent Haidian Innovation Exhibition Center, and the AI Origin Community. During these visits they examined smart city systems and new artificial intelligence tools up close.

The piece presents their observations as key takeaways from this field trip but does not elaborate on specific conclusions or detailed findings beyond noting that the scholars explored these facilities directly to see China's modernization efforts in practice.
items.title: Foreign Scholars Visit Beijing's Innovation Sites to Assess China's Modernization

items.title: International Scholars Describe People-Centered Governance in Beijing

Canada's Supreme Court on Friday largely upheld Quebec's ban on religious symbols for public servants, but ruled that provincial lawmakers should be permitted to wear such symbols in the National Assembly. The court decision concerned Bill 21, which Quebec passed in 2019 and invoked the federal notwithstanding clause over concerns about freedom of religion.

Chief Justice Richard Wagner said the law is rooted in Quebec's legitimate commitment to secularism within a free and democratic society. Mathieu Levesque of the right-wing Coalition Avenir Québec, which passed the bill during its two parliamentary terms from 2018 to 2026 before losing power to the pro-independence Parti Québécois, hailed the ruling as a victory for French-speaking Quebec.

Critics argue the law unfairly targets Muslim women and weakens rights protections. Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said via Reuters that the decision gives every government an unrestricted license to pass legislation stripping Canadians of fundamental freedoms, forcing many Muslim women out of teaching or volunteering in schools. Emmett Macfarlane, head of political science at the University of Waterloo and cited by Reuters, called the law 'Islamophobia as a state policy.'
items.title: Canada Supreme Court Upholds Quebec Secularism Ban

Qatar and Canada reaffirmed their backing of international efforts to aid recovery in Syria and continued cooperation on supporting the Palestinian people during their first Strategic Dialogue held in Ottawa. The talks were co-chaired on Nov. 24 by Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani and Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand under the theme 'Toward Strengthening a Strategic Partnership,' according to a joint communique cited by the Qatar News Agency, with reporting from SANA dated Nov. 28.

The dialogue addressed regional and international developments alongside political, economic, security and humanitarian cooperation, including demands that a Gaza ceasefire be upheld, Israeli forces withdraw, and safe humanitarian aid reach the enclave while preserving UNRWA's role. The two countries renewed support for a just peace based on the two-state solution, rejected annexation of the West Bank, affirmed settlements are illegal, and backed implementing UN Security Council Resolution 2803.

The ministers emphasized de-escalation, dialogue, respect for international law, peaceful dispute settlement, and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab. Bilateral trade exceeded $253 million (355 million Canadian dollars) in 2025, while Qatar's direct investment stock in Canada reached $242 million (339 million Canadian dollars), per the communique.

The countries affirmed continued defense and security cooperation across training, capacity building, military exchanges, defense industries, combating terrorism financing, transnational organized crime, and cyber threats. They agreed to advance their strategic partnership over the coming decade and hold a second Strategic Dialogue in Doha in 2027.
items.title: Qatar and Canada Reaffirm Support for Syria Recovery, Palestinian Rights

Uganda has begun clinical trials of an experimental Moderna mRNA vaccine targeting the Bundibugyo strain responsible for a deadly Ebola outbreak in neighbouring DRC, which the World Health Organization says has killed more than 5,700 people with over 11,000 cases since May. The Uganda Virus Research Institute announced on Friday that it had launched Africa's first mRNA Phase I clinical trial of an investigational vaccine against Bundibugyo ebolavirus in collaboration with Moderna. The study will involve 224 healthy volunteers aged between one and 65 to assess the vaccine's safety and its ability to trigger an immune response, and no vaccines or treatments are currently approved for this strain.

Trials of two experimental vaccines are scheduled to begin on Monday in eastern DRC, targeting people who have been in contact with infected individuals and those considered at high risk. Meanwhile, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, has signed a purchase commitment with India's Serum Institute for 1.5 million doses of the other experimental vaccine developed in collaboration with the University of Oxford, aiming to have hundreds of thousands of doses ready if trials prove successful and the vaccine is approved by the WHO and DRC government. Emanuele Capobianco, Gavi's director of global health security, told AFP he hoped for trials to conclude within the first half of 2027, or even within the first quarter in a more optimistic scenario.

Gavi also holds a stockpile of 500,000 doses of Ervebo, an existing vaccine against the Zaire strain of Ebola, which is being tested to determine whether it is also effective against Bundibugyo. Uganda previously contained imported cases earlier this year and was declared Ebola-free in August after recording 20 infections and two deaths.
items.title: Uganda Begins Africa's First mRNA Ebola Vaccine Trial

Kyiv's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Friday that Ukraine offered a Black Sea ceasefire to enable food exports and passed the details to international allies, adding that Kyiv was waiting for Moscow's response. The announcement came a day after Russia attacked two foreign grain carriers near Odesa overnight; Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi reported the ships carried more than 100,000 metric tons of grain but did not say where the cargo originated or loaded. Sybiha said Kyiv would only consider suspending attacks on Russian oil as part of a broader energy ceasefire deal rather than in isolation.

Grain shipments from Ukraine's key Black Sea ports around Odesa have largely stopped since late July after Russia intensified attacks, and before the escalation those three ports handled about 90 percent of Ukraine's agricultural and metallurgical exports. Shipowners avoid the ports over security risks while soaring insurance costs deter traders, though Kyiv has not formally banned port operations.

Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expressed frustration with the US stance toward Putin in a BBC interview broadcast Friday, calling Trump referring to Putin as 'a friend' strange and likening it to calling Adolf Hitler a friend during World War II. The White House did not respond, while Trump defended his remarks at Mar-a-Lago by saying both leaders hate each other.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Zelensky was insulting his counterpart and showed he is unwilling to follow the path of peace settlement. Nine Ukrainian children were returned Friday from Russia and Russian-occupied territories, including an 8-year-old boy who ran out of a bus at Ukraine's northern border in Chernihiv; some had lost parents who died in occupied territory.

Zelensky announced the latest Bring Kids Back UA operation on social media, thanking US first lady Melania Trump for mediating recent wartime reunifications that so far have brought 43 children home. In all, Ukraine has managed to bring back 2,875 children according to Zelensky.
items.title: Ukraine Submits Black Sea Ceasefire Offer, Awaits Russian Response

items.summary:
In a Guardian column, Jonathan Freedland argues that Donald Trump is elevating himself, favored allies, and the AI industry above legal accountability. He centers his critique on Trump's reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO after revelations about an affair with Alice Huang, whom he says was in regular contact with China's ministry of state security.

Freedland contends that the White House assured Nvidia it did not regard Huang as a national security threat and that no criminal charges were pending. He asserts these assurances should never have been given because they effectively granted Huang immunity from future prosecution, which he compares to a pre-emptive pardon. The columnist notes Trump's own attorney general was vague about whether an investigation had occurred.

He frames this as part of a broader pattern in which Trump uses his office for personal enrichment, citing that Nvidia's value rose after Huang's return and put $15m into Trump's pocket. Freedland also claims the president relies on a 2024 supreme court ruling granting near-blanket immunity for official actions, along with pardon power, to remain functionally immune from consequences.

The columnist concludes that this dynamic extends beyond individuals to the AI sector itself, arguing Trump refuses to regulate datacentres or hold tech leaders accountable. He warns that even as Democrats take control of Congress and subpoena witnesses next week, a president backed by Senate loyalists could simply issue pardons, leaving his aides unpunished.
items.title: Jonathan Freedland accuses Trump of shielding himself and Nvidia's Jensen Huang from the law

items.summary:
The Guardian's editorial argues that the real concern behind reports of AI helping prove the Riemann hypothesis is not the discovery itself but what it reveals about machines outpacing humanity's ability to understand and regulate them. The item states that last Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said he produced a proof for the Riemann hypothesis with assistance from an unreleased version of Claude chatbot, describing it as what many mathematicians see as the holy grail.

The editorial reports that computers can validate the Alpöge-Claude proof but quotes Cornell University's Steven Strogatz fearing AI discoveries may soon defy human understanding. It notes Strogatz said asking AI to explain them would be like trying to teach calculus to his own dog, and separately reported that mathematicians such as students are questioning what is the point if AI can do math better than any human being.

The item states leading mathematicians fear AI has broken or nearly broken encryption safeguarding global finance, communications, and privacy. It reports that in response to the Riemann hypothesis proof, the Bank of England warned unreleased models could be good enough to reverse-engineer calculations underpinning online security, while noting cryptosphere rumours suggest walls will breach within two years.

The editorial states Oxford University's Marcus du Sautoy surprised his interviewer on BBC Radio 4 by wondering if such a breakthrough could already have occurred without public knowledge. It reports that the most consequential mathematical discoveries appear to occur inside privately owned AI labs, with businesses deciding what maths society can know and when breakthroughs are too dangerous to publish. The item notes Donald Trump intervened earlier this year to restrain frontier model spread but states most states lack sufficient independent expertise to assess risks.

The editorial quotes British mathematician IJ Good's 1965 paper envisioning an ultraintelligent machine capable of designing machines more intelligent than itself, and reports that what was considered science fiction is now a key objective of leading AI firms. It concludes by stating the technology exists because humans permit it and argues choices about its concentration of economic power can be unmade.
items.title: Guardian editorial on AI cracking Riemann hypothesis

items.summary:
An MIT study published in Joule examines how excess wind and solar energy could be redirected to power U.S. manufacturing and data centers rather than being wasted through grid curtailment, according to reporting by Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com. The research addresses a growing problem as variable renewable capacity expands: production patterns increasingly conflict with demand, forcing utilities to deliberately cut output from wind and solar farms when supply outstrips need.

The study models the future of U.S. renewables at a point where 80 percent of electricity supplied to consumers comes from solar and wind power, projecting that this would generate 10 percent more energy than the grid can use or store. Lead author Jessika Trancik, a professor in MIT's Institute of Data Systems and Society, said the model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available—generally during spring and fall periods lasting several hours—and aims to help technology developers plan for future infrastructure needs.

The researchers note that current energy storage remains limited, with battery systems able to hold energy only about four hours at a time while long-term solutions are still in research stages. A Zenobe report cited alongside the study highlights insufficient network infrastructure as another barrier, warning that high renewable generation can overload grids and force operators like ESO to pay generators to stop producing electricity, which raises consumer bills and wastes clean energy.
items.title: MIT Study Explores Using Wasted Wind and Solar Power for Factories

items.summary:
Dozens of Labour MPs backing the Rosebank North Sea oilfield are pressuring Prime Minister Andy Burnham not to block the project, warning that refusing could mean 'lights out for Labour in Scotland.' As many as 80 pro-drilling MPs reportedly consider writing their own letter to Burnham after nearly 100 colleagues called on him earlier. Scottish Labour leader Michael Marra reiterated his support and cautioned that working-class vocational jobs are threatened by the North Sea basin's decline, while environment minister Emma Hardy acknowledged the party is split but said Burnham will listen to everyone.

Anti-Rosebank MPs argue the estimated additional 254m tonnes of carbon dioxide Rosebank would produce over its lifetime are not worth the extra £500m in tax receipts and 500 jobs it would generate. Survation polling from last month found that 64% of people in Scotland support UK government approval, with 16% against; analyst PJ Stock noted public backing exists across every age group except 18-to-24-year-olds, where the margin is just a 1% net difference.

Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh technically holds the decision but reportedly leans against approving Rosebank on climate grounds, though most MPs believe she will follow any signal from Burnham. Downing Street said the decision would be taken through a quasi-judicial process considering environmental assessments and consultation representations. If Burnham pushes for approval, he could face resignations over it.
items.title: Labour MPs pressure Burnham over Rosebank oilfield decision

visual.alt: Dot chart. Support approval (64%) 64 %; Against approval (16%) 16 %.
